t: Find the Count of Monotonic Pairs I
o: Count arrays arr1 (non-decreasing), arr2 (non-increasing) with arr1[i]+arr2[i] = nums[i]. Choosing arr1 determines arr2 completely. Example [2,3,2] has 4 valid pairs. n ≤ 2000 but nums[i] ≤ 50, so a DP over positions and arr1 values with prefix sums is required.
k: Fix arr1[i] = v ⇒ arr2[i] = nums[i] − v; monotonicity forces u ≤ v + nums[i−1] − nums[i] for the previous value u.
dp[i][v] = number of valid prefixes with arr1[i] = v; transition is a prefix-sum range query over dp[i−1][0..hi].
Values of v range only over 0..nums[i] (arr2 must stay non-negative).

a.i: For each position, convert the constrained sum over previous arr1 values into a prefix-sum lookup, giving O(n · 50) total.
s: For each next i: build prefix sums of dp; new_dp[v] = prefix(min(v + nums[i−1] − nums[i], nums[i−1]) + 1) if the bound ≥ 0.
Answer = sum of final dp mod 1e9+7.

a.i: When nums is constant (like [5,5,5,5]), the count equals the number of non-decreasing sequences with bounded increments, expressible via binomial coefficients (balls-and-walls with capacity constraints via inclusion–exclusion). General arrays with varying values make this messy, so the DP remains the practical choice; combinatorics serves as a sanity check on uniform inputs.
s: Model gaps d_i = arr1[i] − arr1[i−1] ≥ 0 with upper bounds from nums differences.
Count via inclusion–exclusion over violated bounds.
Compare against DP on small cases.
a.t: O(n + log MOD) for the closed form; O(n·V) fallback

w: Lead with the prefix-sum DP — it handles all inputs uniformly. Sanity-check with [5,5,5,5] → 126 = C(9,4). Pitfalls: off-by-one in the prefix index (hi+1), clamping hi to nums[i−1], and skipping v when hi < 0. Follow-up: version II raises nums[i] to 1000 — same DP still works since it scales with max value.
